claims.text: At approximately fixed 18 wt.% chromium, increasing manganese from about 2 wt.% to about 6 wt.% reduces chromium dissolution from steel in molten fluoride salt.
Higher manganese content promotes formation of stable manganese fluoride compounds in molten fluoride salt.
Formation of manganese fluoride compounds helps preserve a protective chromium-based passive film.
The proposed baseline and modified steels contain about 18 wt.% Cr and respectively about 2 wt.% and 6 wt.% Mn.
Moisture and other salt impurities can affect elemental dissolution and corrosion in molten fluoride salts.
Temperature affects corrosion behavior in molten salts.
The protective surface film in this environment comprises chromium oxides or related chromium compounds.
The integrity of the chromium-containing surface film is maintained when manganese inhibits chromium dissolution.
Formation of MnF2 has a lower Gibbs free energy than formation of CrF2 under the proposed exposure conditions.
Increasing alloy manganese causes preferential or selective manganese dissolution in molten fluoride salt.
Selective manganese dissolution reduces chromium exposure to the aggressive environment.
A persistent, self-healing chromium-based passive layer retards subsequent corrosion in molten fluoride salt.
Relative to the low-manganese baseline, the high-manganese steel will exhibit lower chromium loss to the salt.
Relative to the low-manganese baseline, the high-manganese steel will exhibit lower overall mass loss.
Relative to the low-manganese baseline, the high-manganese steel will exhibit a thicker, more continuous, or otherwise more stable passive film.
The proposed mechanism is limited to high-temperature molten fluoride environments relevant to nuclear and chemical-processing systems.
The proposed mechanism may not operate in aqueous corrosion or ordinary atmospheric oxidation conditions.
The magnitude of protection and film characteristics depend on alloy composition, salt impurities, exposure time, and temperature.

Failure of the high-manganese steel to show a statistically significant improvement in chromium loss, film integrity, or overall mass loss relative to the low-manganese control would falsify the proposed hypothesis.
